summary: Sets the rules for extending the NFSv4 family. It covers creating minor versions, adding optional features to existing minor versions, and fixing flaws in published features. These rules supersede earlier minor versioning rules, including those in RFC 5661, and it updates RFC 5661 and RFC 7862.

plainLanguage.summary: This document is the rule book for how the fourth version of the Network File System can grow new features without breaking the computers that already talk to it. It says which changes can be added to an existing version and which changes force a brand new one.

questions: what is xdr extension in nfsv4
subtitle: How the NFSv4 file protocol can grow through extensions, corrections and new minor versions without breaking old clients.

tldr.problem: NFSv4 needed to evolve, but earlier every change meant a whole new minor version, and the minor versioning rules were scattered and sometimes modified ad hoc in each minor version document.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC consolidates the rules. Compatible XDR extensions, such as new operations or attributes, may be added to an existing minor version as optional features. Changes that are not compatible require a new minor version. Flaws are fixed by adding a corrected alternative beside the old feature.
tldr.outcome: These rules supersede the minor versioning rules in RFC 5661 and other minor version RFCs, and the RFC updates RFC 5661 and RFC 7862. It requires no IANA actions.

facts.label: Supersedes
facts.value: The minor versioning rules in RFC 5661 and the modification in RFC 7862

today: RFC 8178 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5661 and RFC 7862. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the rule set for extending NFSv4.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
To address the requirement for an NFS protocol that can evolve as the need arises, the Network File System version 4 protocol provides a framework to allow for future changes via the creation of new protocol versions, including minor versions and certain forms of modification of existing minor versions. The extension rules contained in this document allow extensions and other changes to be implemented in a way that maintains compatibility with existing clients and servers.

Previously, all protocol changes had been part of new minor versions. The COMPOUND procedure specifies the minor version being used by the client in making requests, and the CB_COMPOUND procedure specifies the minor version being used by the server on callback requests. Creation of a new minor version is no longer the only way in which protocol changes may be made. Optional features may be added as extensions, and protocol corrections can be proposed, specified and implemented within the context of a single minor version. Creation of new minor versions remains available when needed.

The goal of allowing extensions within the context of a minor version is to provide more implementation flexibility while preserving interoperability on protocol upgrade. A client and server may each choose a subset of available extensions, and each party can successfully use a subset of protocol elements that are known to and supported by both the client and server. Support for this common subset is not affected by the fact that extensions outside this common subset may be supported by the server or potentially used by the client.
sections.plainLanguage: Until now, any change to the file protocol meant a whole new version number. This document allows small, compatible additions to be made to a version that already exists.

sections.title: Versions, Minor Versions and Variants
sections.content:
The document uses the terms 'version' and 'minor version' carefully, and defines a 'feature package' as a set of features that are defined together, either as part of a minor version or as part of the same protocol extension.

The term 'version' denotes any valid protocol variant constructed according to the rules in the document. It includes minor versions, but there are situations that allow multiple variant versions to be associated with and coexist within a single minor version. When there are feature specification documents published as Proposed Standards extending a given minor version, then the protocol defined by the minor version specification document, when combined with any subset of the feature specification documents, is a valid NFSv4 version variant that is part of the minor version in question. When there are protocol corrections published that update a given minor version, each set of published updates, up to the date of publication of the update, is a valid NFSv4 version variant that is part of that minor version.

Because of this, there can be multiple version variants within a given minor version. Two have special terms. The base minor version denotes the version variant that corresponds to the minor version as originally defined, including all protocol elements specified in the minor version definition document but not incorporating any extensions or protocol corrections published after that original definition. At any given time, the current minor version denotes the minor version variant including all extensions of and corrections to the minor version made by Standards Track documents published up to that time.

Each client and server that implements a specific minor version implements some particular variant of that minor version, and each variant is a subset of the current minor version and a superset of the base minor version. When the term 'minor version' is used without either of these qualifiers, it refers to something true of all variants within that minor version.
sections.plainLanguage: A minor version can have several shapes. The original shape is the base version, the shape with everything published so far added is the current version, and anything in between is a variant. Every implementation sits somewhere in between.

sections.title: Consolidation of Extension Rules
sections.content:
In the past, the only existing extension rules were the minor versioning rules maintained and specified in the Standards Track RFCs that defined the individual minor versions, and those rules were modified on an ad hoc basis for each new minor version. More recently, minor versioning rules were specified in the NFSv4.1 protocol document while modifications to those rules were allowed in subsequent minor versions.

This document defines a set of extension rules, including rules for minor version construction, and they apply to all future changes to the NFSv4 protocol. The rules are subject to change, but any such change should be part of a Standards Track RFC obsoleting or updating this document. Rather than a single list of extension rules, the document defines multiple sets dealing with the various forms of protocol change: the kinds of changes in XDR definitions that may be made to extend NFSv4, the rules for minor version construction including changes that cannot be made as extensions, and the minor version interaction rules.

The document supersedes minor versioning rules appearing in the minor version specification RFCs, including those in the NFSv4.1 protocol document and the modification to those rules mentioned in the NFSv4.2 protocol document. Conflicts are resolved as follows. The specification of the actual protocols for minor versions previously published as Proposed Standards takes precedence over minor versioning rules in either this document or in the minor version specification RFCs, so if the transition from version A to version B violates a minor versioning rule, the version B protocol stays as it is. Since minor versioning rules 11 and 13 from the NFSv4.1 document deal with the interactions between multiple minor versions, the situation there is more complicated. Otherwise, any conflict between the extension rules in this document and those in minor version specification RFCs is to be resolved based on the treatment in this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules were scattered across several documents and changed from one version to the next. This document gathers them into one place, and says what happens when it disagrees with an older document.

sections.title: XDR Extension
sections.content:
As an extensible XDR-based protocol, NFSv4 has to ensure inter-version compatibility in situations in which the client and server use different XDR descriptions. For example, the client and server may implement different variants of the same minor version, in that they each might add different sets of extensions to the base minor version. The XDR extension paradigm assures that these descriptions are compatible, with clients and servers able to determine and use those portions of the protocol that they both share.

When an NFSv4 version change requires a modification to the protocol XDR, this is effected within a framework based on the idea of XDR extension, in contrast to transitions between major NFS versions, including the one between NFSv3 and NFSv4.0, in which the XDR for one version was replaced by a different XDR for a newer version. The XDR extension approach allows an XDR description to be extended in a way that retains the structure of all previously valid messages.

If a base XDR description is extended to create a second XDR description, three things must be true for the second description to be a valid extension of the first. The set of valid messages described by the extended definition must be a superset of that described by the first. Each message within the set of valid messages described by the base definition must be recognized as having exactly the same structure and interpretation using the extended definition. And each message within the set of messages described as valid by the extended definition but not the base definition must be recognized, using the base definition, as part of an unknown extension.

Within NFSv4, given the central role of COMPOUND and CB_COMPOUND, addition of new RPC procedures is not allowed and the enumeration of operations and callback operations have a special role. Two kinds of XDR extension affect both requests and responses: the addition of previously unspecified operation codes within the framework established by COMPOUND and CB_COMPOUND, and the addition of previously unspecified attributes, which add numeric constants for each attribute's bit position in the attribute bitmap together with XDR typedefs for the attribute format. Other sorts of changes generally affect one of requests, replies, callback or callback replies, and they may determine whether the extension requires a new minor version or can be made within an existing one.

Those other changes are the addition of new, previously unused, values to existing enums, the addition of previously unassigned bit values to a flag word, and the addition of new cases to existing switches, provided that the existing switch did not contain a default case. None of the following is allowed: any change to the structure of existing requests or replies other than those listed; addition of previously unspecified RPC procedures for either the NFSv4 program or the callback program; and deletion of existing RPC procedures, operation codes, enum values, flag bit values and switch cases. Changes may be made to define the use of any of these as causing an error, as long as the XDR is unaffected, and none of these items may be reused for a new purpose.

XDR additions may also be made by defining XDR structures that overlay nominally opaque fields that are defined to allow such incremental extensions, for example where each parallel NFS mapping type provides its own XDR definition for pNFS-related fields defined as opaque arrays.
sections.plainLanguage: A new version of the message format is allowed only if every message that was valid before still reads exactly the same way. New messages must look to an old reader like an extension it does not recognise, so the old reader can safely ignore them.

sections.title: Extending Existing Minor Versions
sections.content:
Extensions to the most recently published NFSv4 minor version may be made by publishing the extension as a Proposed Standard, unless the minor version in question has been defined as non-extensible. A document need not use the 'Updates' header specifying the RFC that defines the minor version, which remains a valid description of the base variant of that minor version.

Such extensions must also obey the XDR extension rules, and must obey further rules to allow interoperability to be established. Additions to the set of callback requests and extensions to the XDR for existing callback operations can only be made if the server can determine, based on the client's actions, that the client is aware of the changes. That determination, for any particular client as defined by its clientid, is made before sending those new or extended callbacks. XDR extensions that affect the structures of responses to existing operations can only be made if the server can determine, based on the client's actions, that the client is aware of the existence of XDR changes, before sending responses containing those extensions. The determination can be based on the request being responded to, but that is not required, and the use of any protocol element defined in the extension can be the basis of it, provided the requirements for determining client awareness are clearly stated.

Corrections to protocol errors may be accomplished by publishing an extension, including a compatible XDR change that follows the rules above, and such documents update the defining documents for the minor version to be corrected.

In some cases extensions contain elements such as new operations or previously invalid switch cases. Although it is possible to determine whether these optional elements are supported using the rules described above, the author of an extension containing such elements has the choice of defining a new attribute that indicates whether the feature is present and supported. Since it is easy to determine whether a new attribute is supported using the supported_attrs attribute, this can make it simple and convenient for clients to determine whether support is present, particularly when a feature involves support for multiple such elements.
sections.plainLanguage: A new feature can be added to the current version, but the server must be able to tell that the client knows about it before using it. A simple way is to publish a new attribute that says whether the feature is there.

sections.title: Minor Version Interaction Rules
sections.content:
Each relationship between a client instance and a server instance, as represented by a clientid, is to be devoted to a single minor version. If a server detects that a COMPOUND with an inappropriate minor version is being used, it MUST reject the request, and in doing so it may return either NFS4ERR_BAD_CLIENTID or NFS4ERR_MINOR_VERS_MISMATCH. As a result, the client has the assurance that the set of required and optional features will not change within the context of a single clientid, and server implementations MUST ensure that the set of supported features and protocol elements does not change within such a context.

The goal of the NFSv4 extension model is to enable compatibility, including compatibility between clients and servers implementing different minor versions. Within a set of minor versions that define the same set of features as required and mandatory to not implement, it is relatively easy for clients and servers to provide the needed compatibility by adhering to a few practices. Servers supporting a given minor version should support earlier minor versions within that set and return appropriate errors for use of protocol elements that were not a valid part of the earlier minor version. Clients should deal with an NFS4ERR_MINOR_VERS_MISMATCH error by searching for a lower minor version number that the server will accept. Servers supporting a given minor version MUST, in returning errors for operations that were a valid part of the minor version, return the errors allowed for the current operation in the minor version actually being used.

With regard to protocol elements not known in a given minor version, the server, although it has a more extensive XDR reflective of a newer minor version, must act as a server with a more limited XDR would. When an operation is used that is not known in the specified minor version, NFS4ERR_OP_ILLEGAL should be returned, as opposed to NFS4ERR_NOTSUPP. When an attribute is used that is not known in the specified minor version, NFS4ERR_INVAL should be returned, as opposed to NFS4ERR_ATTRNOTSUPP. When a switch case is used that is not known in the specified minor version, NFS4ERR_BADXDR should be returned, as opposed to NFS4ERR_UNION_NOTSUPP, even though the message may be XDR-decodable by the server's current XDR. And when a flag bit is used that is not known in the specified minor version, NFS4ERR_INVAL should be returned, as opposed to NFS4ERR_NOTSUPP.
sections.plainLanguage: One connection speaks one version for its whole life. If the server has a newer version, it pretends to have the older one when answering, and it reports anything newer as an error that the older version would have produced.

sections.title: Correction of Existing Minor Versions and Features
sections.content:
The possibility always exists that there will be a need to correct an existing feature in some way after the acceptance of that feature, or of a minor version containing it, as a Proposed Standard. The working group can reduce the probability of such situations by waiting for running code before considering a feature as done, but it cannot reduce the probability to zero, because as features are used more extensively and interact with other features, previously unseen flaws may be discovered. Such corrections are best done in a document obsoleting or updating the RFC defining the relevant feature or minor version, and the working group will have to consider carefully how to assure interoperability with older clients and servers.

Often, corrections can be done without changing the protocol XDR. In many cases a change in client and server behavior can be implemented without special provision for interoperability with earlier implementations, and a new document can be published that simply updates the earlier protocol definition document. In other cases it is best if client or server behavior needs to change in a way that raises interoperability concerns, and in such cases incompatible changes in server or client behavior should not be mandated in order to avoid XDR changes.

When XDR changes are necessary as part of correcting a flaw, they should be done in a manner similar to that used when implementing new minor versions or features within them. Existing XDR structures may not be modified or deleted. XDR extensions may be used to correct existing protocol facilities in a manner similar to those used to add additional optional features, and such corrections may be done in a minor version for which optional features may no longer be added, if the working group decides that it is an appropriate way to compatibly effect a correction.

A correction to an optional feature leaves the protocol in a situation similar to one in which there are two independent optional features, and a server may choose to implement either or both. A correction to a required feature leaves the old version of the feature required while the corrected version, while optional, is intended to be adopted to provide correct operation. Use of the corrected version is ultimately better and may be recommended, but it should not be described as 'RECOMMENDED' since the choice of versions to support depends on the needs of clients, which may be slow to adopt the updated version. In all of these cases it is appropriate that the old version of the feature be considered obsolescent, with the expectation that the working group might, in a later minor version, change the status of the uncorrected version.

For a correction to a required feature there are several less disruptive changes that could be made earlier: changing the uncorrected version from required to optional while requiring that servers support at least one of the two versions, which allows new server implementations to avoid support for the uncorrected version; changing the corrected version from optional to required, making both versions required, which allows new clients to depend on support for the corrected version being present; and changing the uncorrected version from required to optional while changing the corrected version from optional to required, which completes the shift once clients are prepared to use the corrected version.
sections.plainLanguage: When a published feature turns out to be wrong, the fix is added alongside the old version rather than replacing it, so old and new clients can still talk to each other. The old version is retired only in a later version.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Since no substantive protocol changes are proposed in the document, no security considerations apply. The IANA Considerations section states that the document does not require any IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: The document changes no messages and adds no numbers, so it brings no security issues of its own.

viz.caption: THE THREE NAMES FOR A VERSION (RFC 8178, SECTION 2.3)

cells: The minor version as originally defined, with no later extensions or corrections.
The minor version variant including all extensions and corrections published up to now.
Any point in between. Each implementation uses one, a subset of the current version and a superset of the base version.

viz.caption: WHAT AN XDR EXTENSION MAY AND MAY NOT DO (RFC 8178, SECTIONS 4.1 AND 4.2)

items.title: Add operation codes
items.text: New operation codes and new attributes may be added within the framework of COMPOUND and CB_COMPOUND.

items.title: Extend enumerations
items.text: New values may be added to existing enums, new bits to a flag word, and new cases to a switch that has no default case.

items.title: Keep old messages intact
items.text: Every message valid under the old description must have exactly the same structure under the new one.

items.title: No new procedures
items.text: New RPC procedures may not be added, and existing procedures, operation codes, enum values, flag bits and switch cases may not be deleted or reused.

cells: The corrected and uncorrected versions become two independent optional features, and a server may implement either or both.
The uncorrected version stays required, while the corrected version is optional and intended to be adopted.
A later minor version can make the uncorrected version optional, or make the corrected one required, or do both.
